section_1.title: Introduction: The Trust Problem
section_1.content: Define the challenge of digital scarcity without a central authority. Introduce the core triad: Cryptographic Hashing, Asymmetric Encryption, and Probabilistic Proof-of-Work.
section_1.example: Imagine 'Digital Squirrels' trying to agree on how many nuts are in a shared hollow tree without a head squirrel counting them.

section_2.title: Cryptographic Hashing: The Digital Fingerprint
section_2.content: Explain SHA-256 as a one-way function: f(x) = y. Visualize this as a 'digital blender' where inputting a document results in a unique, fixed-length hex string that cannot be reversed.
section_2.example: Input: 'Apple' -> Blender -> Output: 'a5c9...'. If you change it to 'apple' (lowercase), the output changes entirely, demonstrating the 'avalanche effect'.

section_3.title: Asymmetric Cryptography: Digital Ownership
section_3.content: Introduce the math of Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC). Explain the concept of a Private Key (a large random integer) and a Public Key (a point on a curve derived via scalar multiplication).
section_3.example: A 'Magic Key' (Private) creates a 'Lock' (Public). Anyone can see the lock, but only the specific key can turn it to sign a transaction.

section_4.title: Proof of Work: The Lottery of Consensus
section_4.content: Explain the mining process as a mathematical race to find a 'nonce' that makes the block hash start with a specific number of zeros. This requires immense computational energy, making tampering prohibitively expensive.
section_4.example: A robot trying millions of combinations to open a combination lock; the first one to find the sequence '0000' wins the right to add the block.

section_5.title: The Mathematical Security of the Chain
section_5.content: Summarize how these components link together. Conclude with the visual of the 'Blockchain' as a chain of blocks where each block contains the hash of the previous one, creating an immutable history.
section_5.example: If a hacker tries to change a transaction in block 1, the 'fingerprint' of every subsequent block breaks, notifying the entire network instantly.
